title: Don't Compete on Price When You Own the Platform

sourceCase: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech)
lessonTitle: Don't Compete on Price When You Own the Platform
situation: In February 2009, Google ad-serving rival Atlas offered Hewlett-Packard $0.015 CPM — well below Google's $0.025 floor — to keep HP's ad-serving business. Agencies (GroupM, OMD, Havas, WPP) started using that rate as leverage in their own renewals. Internally, Neal Mohan, David Rosenblatt, and the DoubleClick sales team debated whether to hold price or fold.
insight: Two moves stand out. First, Ruth Kirschner refuses to reset the floor for one deal: HP is 'annoyingly telling each shop' about the $0.015 rate, but she reads Atlas's pricing as desperation, not the new normal, and bets on 'global capabilities' as the reason to hold premium. Second, Neal Mohan reframes the whole fight for Patrick: comparing DoubleClick as a standalone business on CPM per impression is 'silly' because 'the strategic battleground in display is publisher platform (ie, inventory).' Translation: ad-serving fees are the visible price, but the real prize is controlling publisher inventory. Losing a few basis points on CPM is fine if it buys platform position. This is classic **loss-leader logic inside a platform strategy** — you don't defend the toll booth, you defend the road.
application: When a competitor undercuts you, ask two questions before matching: Is their price a signal of strength or of desperation? And is the thing they're cutting the thing that actually matters to your business? If the discounted product is really a gateway to a larger platform or relationship, price it to win the gateway — and communicate the bigger value story to customers using the low price as leverage.
pullQuote: When a rival slashes prices out of desperation, the answer isn't matching them — it's reminding your customers what game you're actually playing.
